title: Laylat al-Qadr
hookLine: in Ramadan's last nights, Muslims pray for forgiveness on the Night of Power (Quran 97)

cards: It's past midnight near the end of Ramadan, and the mosque is still lit. Some people stand in prayer. Some sit against the wall with the Qur'an open on their knees.
Some have brought blankets and will stay until dawn. At home, others pray quietly in a back room while the house sleeps. Nobody knows for certain which of these nights is the one they're looking for.
That's part of it. The night has a name, and a whole short chapter of the Qur'an to itself. Laylat al-Qadr: the Night of Power.

teach.h: WE REVEALED IT ON THIS NIGHT.
teach.b: First, what the Qur'an says. Surah ninety-seven is short. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power."
Muslims understand it to be the Qur'an, first sent down on this night.
Then a startling comparison: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Second, how it ends.
The angels and the Spirit come down, the chapter says, and the night is "Peace until the rising of the dawn." Not a night of fear or judgment: a night of peace. Third, the hiding.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told his followers to seek the night in the last nights of Ramadan, the odd-numbered ones, according to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.
That hadith gives no single date, so people keep watch across several nights. Some readers see the hiding as a mercy of its own: it keeps people praying longer. Fourth, the question his wife asked.
In a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, Aisha asks him what she should say if she knows which night it is.

teach.h: YOU LOVE TO PARDON, SO PARDON ME.
teach.b: He teaches her a short supplication, in paraphrase: God, you are the one who pardons, and you love to pardon, so pardon me.
Of all the things to ask for on a night better than a thousand months, the answer he gives is forgiveness.

how: Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr in the last nights of Ramadan with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and supplication, and the supplication the Prophet taught Aisha, asking God to pardon, is said on those nights.

o: the night of the Prophet's journey to Jerusalem
the feast that ends the month of Ramadan with prayer
the Night of Power, when the Qur'an was first sent down

games.q: the Night of Power — tap the pairs.
p: until the rising of the dawn
what to say on that night

s: the Qur'an gives the exact date of the Night of Power
the date is hidden; a hadith says to seek it in the last, odd-numbered nights of Ramadan.
Surah 97 calls the night better than a thousand months
"The Night of Power is better than a thousand months."
the Prophet taught Aisha to ask for wealth on that night
he taught her to ask God, who loves to pardon, to pardon her.

games.q: you're Aisha. you ask the Prophet what to say if you find the Night of Power. what does he teach you to ask for?
o: pardon from God, who loves to pardon.
games.why: in al-Tirmidhi's collection, he teaches a short supplication asking God, who pardons and loves to pardon, to pardon her.

practice: Let these minutes be a small night watch, whatever the hour, and bring to mind the first thing you'd ask to be forgiven for, without explaining or defending it.

Then, in your own way, ask: if you pray, with the words of your own tradition, or, if you're Muslim, the words the Prophet taught Aisha. If you don't pray, simply let yourself want it to be let go, and stay with that wanting.

wordCard.voice: Laylat al-Qadr. The Night of Power, in the last nights of Ramadan, when the Qur'an was first revealed and Muslims keep watch and ask forgiveness. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, Qur'an 97:1: the Night of Power, also translated the Night of Decree.

carryVoice: Your line: the night of power. A night of peace, until the dawn. That's day nine hundred ninety-six.
